reading.title: Five Pairs That Trick Writers
reading.purpose: Learn simple memory tricks to tell apart five commonly confused English word pairs.
paras: Some English words look and sound so much alike that even careful writers mix them up. A quick trick for each pair makes choosing the right spelling easy.

Start with advice and advise. Advice, with a c, is a noun naming helpful tips you receive. Advise, with an s, is an action word meaning to tell someone what you think they should do. Notice the same noun-and-verb pattern in breath and breathe: you take a deep breath of cool air, and you breathe in and out with an extra e at the end.
Next, watch lose and loose. If you lose your house key, you cannot find it; you can also lose a chess match. Loose, with two o's, means not tight, like a shoelace that needs a knot.

Now check farther and further. Use farther for a real distance you can measure, such as throwing a ball farther across a field. Use further when you mean "more," such as looking further into a science question.

Last, compare compliment and complement. A compliment with an i is kind praise, like saying "I like your painting." To complement with an e means to go well together and complete something, the way crisp apples complement warm cheddar cheese.

choices: to go well together and complete something
to say something kind about a friend's art
to throw a baseball across a grassy field
to take a deep gulp of cool morning air
qs.why: Paragraph 5 explains that complement with an e means "to go well together and complete something."

qs.q: Which sentence tells when to use the word "farther"?
choices: Use farther for a real distance you can measure, such as throwing a ball farther across a field.
Use further when you mean "more," such as looking further into a science question.
qs.why: This sentence explains that farther is used for a real distance you can measure.

ev.text: Use farther for a real distance you can measure, such as throwing a ball farther across a field.

qs.q: Eli's bike chain is not tight enough and keeps slipping off the gear. Which word from the reading describes the bike chain?
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that loose, with two o's, means not tight.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: English words with two o's are always harder to spell than short verbs.
Simple rules help writers tell apart five pairs of look-alike words.
Kind praise is more helpful to a writer than studying a spelling list.
Every noun in English turns into a verb when you add the letter e.
qs.why: The reading introduces five commonly confused pairs and gives a clear rule for telling each pair apart.
